text: Hubert Dreyfus's critique of classical (GOFAI) artificial intelligence, drawing on Heidegger and Merleau-Ponty, held that...
choices: human intelligence can be fully captured by explicit symbolic rules given sufficient memory
the Turing test is too easy because human judges are biased and easily fooled
intelligent human coping depends on embodied, practical know-how that cannot be reduced to explicit rules or representations
machines cannot think because God did not endow them with immortal souls
explanation: Dreyfus argued in What Computers Can't Do (1972) that skilled human coping rests on embodied, situated know-how that resists formalization into explicit rules, the core weakness of rule-based GOFAI. Option A is the GOFAI assumption he rejects; B is a Loebner-style objection; D is Turing's 'theological objection,' not Dreyfus's.
